scope: Six original AQA AS Physics 3.3.2.3 plane refraction and step-index optical fibre applications (37 marks)
notes: Original text and point rubrics, not published AQA questions or official mark schemes. All ray-diagram points require manual inspection, never automatic word-only marking. Check equivalent numerical rounding and alternative methods manually.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style AS Step-index Refraction and Fibre Applications
questions.question: Critical angle and step-index cladding
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: A step-index optical fibre has core refractive index 1.50 and cladding refractive index 1.47. A ray inside the core reaches the core–cladding boundary at an angle of incidence of 80.0° to the normal. Calculate the critical angle and decide whether total internal reflection occurs. Explain TWO separate purposes of cladding. [6 marks]
markPoints: Correctly identifies core as the higher-index medium and cladding as lower-index medium.
States sin θc=nclad/ncore.
Substitutes sin θc=1.47/1.50=0.980.
Calculates θc≈78.5° (accept suitable rounding).
States 80.0°>78.5°, so total internal reflection occurs.
Explains lower-index cladding enables reflection at the core boundary AND protects the core surface from damage/light leakage.
questions.modelAnswer: Core n₁=1.50>cladding n₂=1.47. sinθc=n₂/n₁=1.47/1.50=0.980, θc=78.52° (≈78.5°). Since the core ray arrives at 80.0°>θc, it is totally internally reflected. The lower cladding index maintains the reflecting boundary; cladding also protects the core surface from scratches that can cause light leakage.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style AS Step-index Refraction and Fibre Applications
questions.question: Snell refraction and light speed in a medium
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: A narrow ray of light passes from air (n=1.00) into a transparent material (n=1.50) with an incidence angle of 30.0° to the normal. Calculate the refraction angle and the speed of light inside the material. Use c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹. State whether the ray bends towards or away from the normal. [6 marks]
markPoints: States Snell's law n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂.
Calculates θ₂≈19.5° (accept 19.47°).
States n=c/v or v=c/n.
Calculates v=3.00×10⁸/1.50=2.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹ with units.
Explains the ray bends towards the normal as it enters the higher-index medium.
questions.modelAnswer: Using Snell's law, n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂, so sinθ₂=1.00×sin30.0°/1.50=1/3 and θ₂=19.47°≈19.5°. The speed is v=c/n=3.00×10⁸/1.50=2.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹. The refracted angle decreases and the ray bends towards the normal.

questions.series: Original AQA-style AS Step-index Refraction and Fibre Applications
questions.question: Material dispersion pulse arrival-time difference
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: A short light pulse travels 1.20 km through a fibre core. At a blue wavelength the core index is 1.467 and at a red wavelength it is 1.459. Treat both path lengths as 1.20 km. Use c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹. Calculate the propagation time for each colour and their arrival-time difference. State which arrives first and explain the effect on digital information pulses. [7 marks]
markPoints: Converts L=1.20 km to 1.20×10³ m.
Uses v=c/n and hence t=Ln/c.
Finds time difference 3.20×10⁻⁸ s (32.0 ns).
States red arrives first because its refractive index is lower and speed is higher.
Explains different wavelengths spread the pulse in time (material dispersion), causing possible overlap/confusion of adjacent data pulses.
questions.modelAnswer: L=1200m and v=c/n, so t=Ln/c. Blue: t=1200×1.467/(3.00×10⁸)=5.868×10⁻⁶s. Red: t=1200×1.459/(3.00×10⁸)=5.836×10⁻⁶s. Δt=3.20×10⁻⁸s=32.0ns. Red arrives first. Different wavelength components travel at different speeds, broadening the pulse so neighbouring digital bits may overlap.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style AS Step-index Refraction and Fibre Applications
questions.question: Explain modal dispersion, material dispersion and absorption
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: Two types of pulse broadening can affect light signals in a step-index optical fibre. Distinguish modal dispersion from material dispersion. Explain how absorption differs from dispersion, and give two reasons why pulse broadening can limit transmission quality or bit rate. [6 marks]
markPoints: Modal dispersion arises because different rays/modes travel paths of different lengths.
Some longer ray paths cause later arrival than shorter paths, broadening the pulse.
Material dispersion arises because different wavelength components have different refractive indices/speeds.
Absorption reduces transmitted light energy/intensity (signal attenuation), rather than directly explaining the arrival-time spread.
Pulse broadening can make successive pulses overlap.
Overlapping pulses can be harder to distinguish, causing errors or limiting the maximum bit rate.
questions.modelAnswer: Modal dispersion occurs when rays take different-length paths through a step-index fibre, so longer paths arrive later. Material dispersion occurs when wavelengths travel at different speeds because of differing refractive indices. Absorption attenuates the signal by removing optical energy and reducing received intensity, whereas dispersion broadens the pulse. Broadening risks overlap of adjacent pulses, limiting the maximum reliable bit rate.

questions.question: Draw and label core–cladding total internal reflection
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: Draw a labelled ray diagram showing a light ray inside a step-index fibre core striking the boundary with the cladding at an angle of incidence of 82°. The core index is 1.51 and the cladding index is 1.48. Calculate the critical angle and show the ray's correct path, the normal, and its direction after the boundary. The sketch must be manually reviewed; a written description alone cannot earn the drawing marks. [6 marks]
markPoints: Sketch correctly distinguishes the higher-index core n=1.51 from lower-index cladding n=1.48.
Draws and labels a normal perpendicular to the core–cladding interface at the impact point.
Draws the incident ray in the core approaching the boundary and labels incidence 82° relative to the normal.
Calculates θc=arcsin(1.48/1.51)≈78.6° and states 82°>θc.
Draws a reflected ray remaining inside the core at 82° to the normal on the opposite side, consistent with reflection law.
Shows no propagating refracted ray continuing through the cladding, and correctly labels total internal reflection.
questions.modelAnswer: sinθc=1.48/1.51=0.980132..., so θc≈78.56°. A ray arriving at 82° relative to the boundary normal undergoes TIR. In the sketch, draw an interface between core (n=1.51) and cladding (n=1.48), draw a normal perpendicular to the boundary, and show the core incident ray meeting the boundary and the reflected ray inside the core making 82° on the other side of the normal. Label the TIR; no transmitted geometric ray is drawn. Diagram marks require human review.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style AS Step-index Refraction and Fibre Applications
questions.question: Why a higher cladding index can prevent light guidance
questions.subtopic: Refraction, critical angle, step-index cladding, material/modal dispersion
questions.prompt: Consider a step-index fibre with fixed core refractive index 1.50. Initially its cladding index is 1.45. A redesign raises the cladding index to 1.49. Calculate the original and revised critical angles at the core–cladding interface. Explain whether a core ray incident at 80.0° would show total internal reflection in each design and why. [6 marks]
markPoints: Uses sinθc=nclad/ncore with ncore=1.50.
Original θc=arcsin(1.45/1.50)≈75.2°.
Revised θc=arcsin(1.49/1.50)≈83.4°.
Correctly states 80.0°>75.2°, so the original design gives TIR.
Correctly states 80.0°<83.4°, so the revised design does not give TIR.
Explains moving the cladding index closer to the core raises the critical angle, making TIR harder to achieve for a given ray direction.
questions.modelAnswer: The critical angle has sinθc=ncladding/ncore. Initially sinθc=1.45/1.50 and θc=75.16°. Afterwards sinθc=1.49/1.50 and θc=83.38°. A ray at 80.0° exceeds the original critical angle, so it is totally internally reflected there. It is below the new critical angle, so it is refracted into the cladding in the revised design. Increasing ncladding towards ncore raises θc.
